title: Keras `__init__.py` structure isn't readable by a static type checker
body:
In keras 3.2.1, if you import say keras.models, you get no errors in VS code:

![image](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/assets/19672699/21a37f87-b742-4222-9486-a8c6baa79c9d)

In keras 3.3.1, this same code shows an error:

![image](https://github.com/keras-team/keras/assets/19672699/475ef543-7220-4d66-85d3-8bf5ad618612)

I believe the reason for this was the refactoring of the `__init__.py` that happened in this commit:

https://github.com/keras-team/keras/commit/04891e89da87c2a433beb12ff7dad59403c71671

The code added in this commit dynamically adds the path to `api` to the sys path. This isn't something a static type checker can handle. 

Could this change be reverted? Or perhaps marked with a `if TYPECHECKING` special case?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Sorry I should have said, the code runs fine, it just can't be interpreted by a static type checker. Our users are confused by this because they can execute their code just fine, but Pylance doesn't think there's a module called `keras.models`.  This makes it harder for them to write code using `keras.models` because there's no intellisense for it anymore.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: @participant2 @participant7 can we resolve this?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> The code added in this commit dynamically adds the path to api to the sys path. This isn't something a static type checker can handle.

Basically, publicly-exported APIs are in `keras/api/`, rather than in the top-level `keras/` folder. This is not unlike, e.g. TF APIs, which live in `tf._api.v2`. Can PyLance only handle packages where the directory structure matches the public namespace?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> Can PyLance only handle packages where the directory structure matches the public namespace?

We should be able to handle anything that's through static imports. The old code was importing all of the api modules, so Pylance could tell that those were imported in the `__init__.py`.

The code in the commit I referenced changed to add the api path to the sys.path at runtime. We don't execute any python code, so we can't actually figure out that api should be on the sys.path.

It's kind of similar to how we [don't](https://microsoft.github.io/pyright/#/import-resolution?id=editable-installs) support [PEP 660](https://peps.python.org/pep-0660/) because we can't execute the dynamic code in the `.pth` files. 

Here's a similar example:
https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/issues/6272

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
We also have a [problem ](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/issues/3753) with tensorflow too when it imports keras like this:

```
from tensorflow.keras import activations, initializers, layers, losses, metrics, models, optimizers, regularizers
```

This is because keras is added to the tensorflow package dynamically.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: @reporter can you say more about the `if TYPECHECKING` special case?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I'd be happy to. 

If you've never seen it before, it's described here:
https://typing.readthedocs.io/en/latest/spec/directives.html#type-checking

It basically tells type checkers extra information that the runtime doesn't care about. 

So you might for example have this in your `__init__.py`

```python

if typing.TYPE_CHECKING:
  from keras.api import _tf_keras
  from keras.api import activations
  from keras.api import applications
  from keras.api import backend
  from keras.api import callbacks
  from keras.api import config
  from keras.api import constraint
  # etc
else:
   # Import everything from /api/ into keras.
   from keras.api import *  # noqa: F403
   from keras.api import __version__  # Import * ignores names start with "_".

   # Add everything in /api/ to the module search path.
   __path__.append(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "api"))  # noqa: F405
```

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Thanks!

I guess if the issue is just with `import *`, we can probably just make sure we individually import everything from api -> toplevel. I don't think this needs to be done with `if TYPE_CHECKING` at all. We could even extend our api gen script to generate that block in the `__init__.py` file. @reporter @participant1 does that sounds like a plan?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Sounds like a plan! This is clean solution.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
I found a simple workaround.
You can import the same objects from `keras.api` and its submodules. Pylance correctly works with such imports, and intellisense fully works.
For example, replace `from keras.optimizers import SGD` with `from keras.api.optimizers import SGD`

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
I'm sorry I wasn't there when this was open, as I had the same problem during the development of my packages.

In short, the reason pylance doesn't recognize exported symbols is because it doesn't follow the Python convention for public symbol interfaces.

you can read it [here](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/distributing.html#library-interface-public-and-private-symbols)

To solve this you have two ways to do it

1. create the `__all__` symbol that will contain all the public symbols of the module or package
```python
# keras/__init__.py
from ... import activations, applications, ...

__all__ = (
    "activations",
    "applications",
    "backend",
    ...  # all the symbols that will be public
)
```
2. Imports should use a redundant alias (this tells type checkers to treat them as public, since they are private by default)
```python
from ... import activations as activations
from ... import applications as applications
...
```

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
This api/src division is causing problems and breaks conventions. It breaks IDE autocompletion and import resolution and forces developers to implement hacks or use non-standard imports and creates unnecessary confusion

`pytorch`, `numpy` and other major libraries separate implementation from API without breaking standard import patterns.
Can we please consider reverting to a conventional package structure so all linting and analysis tools just work out of the box. 

These kinds of imports should work seamless in vscode and other ides but don't:

`from keras.layers import Dense`

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Yeah let's fix this, this is pretty broken. `from keras import layers` needs to not appear broken with typecheckers.

@participant5 thanks for the note, I think the redundant alias is probably a good fit for us.

I also think we need should ditch the `__path__` shenanigans at the top level init. We *do* want a separate exported api structure (this is important). Ideally, we don't want the toplevel browsing experience of our github repo to be a bunch of empty directories and init files (nice to have, not essential). But I think we can get everything we want with standard packaging tools (setuptools `package_dirs`) so the packaged version of Keras does not the `api/` redirection and the public modules are where you'd expect.

I'll work on proposing a change with the redundant alias suggestion. Definitely we can find something that keeps our explicit api surface, and satisfies the typecheckers.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Ok, here's a possible fix. Added the redudant export names, though I think the big issue might be the `__path__` hacking in the package `__init__` that would trip up IDEs and the like -- that's gone too.

The `api/` structure is now purely on the github site, package side we have.

```python
keras
├── activations
│   └── __init__.py
....  # Public init files with redundant imports.
├── src
....  # Private stuff subject to API changes.
```

If folks are able to test this out much appreciated! Particular with typechecking and development setups you are using. I pushed a package to a [keras-test](https://pypi.org/project/keras-test/) name on pypi.

Any of these (probably all good to check):
`pip install keras-test`
`pip install git+https://github.com/participant2/keras@participant8`
`git clone https://github.com/participant2/keras -b fix-package && pip install -e keras`

https://github.com/keras-team/keras/compare/master...participant2:fix-package
